sentences.text: The single known specimen shares the basic body proportions of young tyrannosaurids, including a large skull, long legs built for running, and very small two-fingered forelimbs.
This juvenile individual was approximately 3 meters long and weighed 65 kilograms.
The holotype specimen, identified as LH PV18, measured approximately 2.5 meters and died at the age of three years.
The genus name Raptorex is derived from the Latin words for 'robber' and 'king'.
The genus Raptorex was described in 2009 by Sereno and colleagues.
The holotype fossil is designated LH PV18 and is housed in the Long Hao Institute of Geology and Paleontology in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, China.
The type species R. kriegsteini was described in 2009 by Sereno to honor Roman Kriegstein, a Holocaust survivor who donated the specimen to the University of Chicago.
The holotype fossil LH PV18 was acquired from a Mongolian fossil seller by an American dealer in Tokyo, Japan, and later transported to the United States.
Henry Kriegstein notified the American paleontologist Paul Sereno about the specimen.
Newbrey et al. identified the fish vertebra found with the holotype as belonging to a hiodontid, suggesting the specimen comes from the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation.
Kim et al. (2022) compared the fish centrum with species from the Nemegt Formation, supporting the conclusion that the holotype comes from that formation.
Raptorex is classified as a controversial genus of tyrannosaurid dinosaur.
Raptorex has been successively interpreted as a tyrannosaurid, a tyrannosauroid, and a synonym of Tarbosaurus.
It is generally classified as a tyrannosauroid that is more advanced than Bagaraatan but less advanced than Dryptosaurus.
The parent group of Raptorex is Tyrannosauroidea.
The type species of the genus Raptorex is Raptorex kriegsteini.
Raptorex lived during the Upper Cretaceous period.
Raptorex lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
The time range for Raptorex is from the Barremian to the Maastrichtian, spanning 125.77 to 66 million years ago.
Sereno initially claimed the specimen belonged to the Early Cretaceous based on index fossils found in the surrounding rock slab.
Sereno initially claimed to the press that index fossils surrounding the specimen indicated it belonged to the Early Cretaceous.
However, only a single fish vertebra and an unidentified crushed mollusk shell were found alongside the Raptorex specimen.
Raptorex was initially thought to be from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation approximately 125 million years ago, but later studies found this date unlikely.
Later studies indicated that the specimen's initial age assignment was improbable and that it likely originated from the Iren Dabasu Formation in Mongolia or a similar formation.
Many researchers consider Raptorex a nomen dubium because the growth changes in tyrannosaurids are not well understood, preventing confident pairing with adult skeletons.

Many researchers now consider Raptorex a nomen dubium because it is a juvenile and cannot be securely compared to an adult skeleton, despite resembling juvenile Tarbosaurus bataar of the same age and size.
It is debated whether Raptorex is a valid genus or possibly synonymous with Tarbosaurus bataar due to similarities in juvenile skeletons.
In 2026, Raun and colleagues argued that the diagnostic features of Raptorex are also found in juvenile Tarbosaurus, suggesting Raptorex is a junior synonym of Tarbosaurus.
In October 2010, a non-peer-reviewed report published in Nature News challenged the classification of Raptorex as a basal tyrannosauroid.
